Malleable

MAL-ee-uh-bul · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Malleable is capable of being shaped, molded, or hammered into a new form; easily influenced or changed.

The metalworking apprentice learned to heat the copper sheet until it grew malleable enough to hammer into the curved shape of the lamp's base.

Worked Example

Marketing researchers often describe teenage brand loyalty as highly malleable, since a single viral trend can completely reshape what an entire generation considers cool.

Malleable can describe a physical material shaped by pressure or heat, or -- just as often -- a person, mind, or situation with real potential to be changed or developed.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

moldable: capable of being formed into a new shape

adaptable: capable of adjusting to new conditions

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

rigid: stiff and unable to change shape

unyielding: refusing to change or bend

Where it sits · how loosely its shape is fixed — workable → malleable → formless

workable vs. malleable: Workable just means usable for a task -- it doesn't emphasize an ongoing capacity to be reshaped, the way malleable does.

formless vs. malleable: Formless goes even further than malleable, describing something that hasn't taken on any fixed shape at all yet.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — malle-

root — malle-: hammer (Latin malleus)

suffix — -able

suffix — -able: able to be (Latin -abilis)

Put it together

Put it together: Malleable comes from Latin malleus ('hammer') -- the same root behind the everyday tool mallet. Something malleable is, at root, able to be hammered into a new shape without breaking.

Use the root in a new word: mallet

Use the root in a new word: mallet: The judge's mallet came down with a sharp crack, calling the courtroom to order.

Root Check

Word Choice

Malleable is usually neutral or even positive -- it suggests real potential for growth or change, especially when describing young minds, new organizations, or raw materials, rather than criticizing weakness.
